messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miriam Taufa is a 58-year-old divorced woman of Tongan descent who serves as a rabbi at a mid-sized congregation in the Pacific Northwest. She came to the clinic carrying a PCL-5 score of 78, describing herself in the intake paperwork as someone she no longer recognises. The event that fractured her sense of self occurred fourteen months ago, when the vehicle she was driving was struck by a fuel tanker that ran a red light. Her car spun into a guardrail and caught fire. Miriam was conscious throughout — she remembers the smell of burning plastic and fuel filling the cabin, the heat against her face, and the sound of her own screaming before a bystander pulled her free. She escaped with burns to her forearms and a shattered left wrist, but she has never fully left that intersection.

In the weeks following the accident, Miriam found that certain sensory details had become portals back into the burning car. The smell of anything scorched — a forgotten pan on the stove, the incense sometimes used at interfaith services she attended — would drop her immediately back into that moment of helpless terror. Trauma-related events on the congregational calendar, such as memorial services for accident victims or pastoral visits to hospital burn units, carried the same gravitational pull. Even waking from a nightmare, still damp with sweat and heart hammering, was enough to keep her body convinced the danger had not passed. These triggers reliably activated a state of physiological alarm: she became irritable and snapped at her cantor and administrative staff in ways that left her ashamed, and she had begun taking risks that puzzled even her — driving too fast on rain-slicked roads, as though daring fate to finish what it had started. When someone touched her shoulder unexpectedly during a service, she flinched so violently that a congregant stepped back in alarm.

The threat state, once activated, fed directly back into the landscape of danger. Her heightened startle and the angry outbursts kept her nervous system primed, so that ordinary moments — a car backfiring, a congregant approaching from behind — read as emergencies requiring re-scanning. This constant vigilance made her more sensitive to the very cues she was trying to outrun, and the cycle tightened. The burnt smell, the residue of nightmares, the trauma-laden pastoral work she could not entirely avoid: all of it arrived with greater force because her body was already braced.

What Miriam had developed to manage this were strategies that made sense in the short term and cost her dearly over months. When a trigger struck, she would cover her face with her hands — a gesture that had begun as something almost involuntary but had become a visible habit her staff had quietly started to work around. She forced herself to think only positive thoughts, rehearsing blessings and gratitude in a kind of internal chant that kept her from processing what had actually happened to her. She had also begun eating excessively in the evenings, working through the contents of her refrigerator after Shabbat services in a fog of distress she could not name. These strategies, over time, prevented any real integration of the traumatic material; the suppressed images pressed back harder, and the forced positivity collapsed each time a nightmare broke through, leaving her more disoriented than before. The very rituals meant to contain distress became new triggers — the act of covering her face, the frantic reframing — signalling to her body that something threatening was still present.

What frightened Miriam most was what she had come to believe about herself. She felt profoundly isolated from her congregation, from her adult children in Auckland, from the woman who had stood at a bimah for thirty years and held other people's grief with steadiness. She was certain that her body had become her enemy, reacting with alarms she could neither justify nor silence. The sense that she was unrecognisable to herself — that the person who flinched, overate, and snapped at colleagues was not the rabbi she had built her life around being — deepened the threat she perceived in every interaction, and that deepened threat made the triggers more potent, and so the loop continued. She sought help when she cancelled a family bereavement service because she could not face the smell of memorial candles, and a senior congregant gently asked if she was all right. She was not. What she is most hoping for, she said quietly at the end of the intake, is to feel like herself again.
